Q174.L1t: The passage is a short story about a man named Luca who dreams of reaching a secret Island of Inventions.
Q174.L2t: In the story, Luca and the other young inventors all hoped to be sent an invitation letter to the Island.
Q174.L3t: The passage says that the disappointment of not getting the letter led to even greater cooperation and help among the inventors, and that they did not lose heart but kept learning and inventing to come up with better ideas.
Q174.L4t: Not receiving the letter made them feel disappointed, but that disappointment pushed them to cooperate more and work harder at their inventions.
Q174.L2f: In the story, Luca first heard about the Island of Inventions from a letter sent by a famous inventor when he was already an old man.
Q174.L3f: The passage says that after no letter came, the inventors stopped waiting quietly and began showing their inventions to the world to win attention and an invitation.
Q174.L4f: Because the letter never came, the inventors changed their approach and began to promote their inventions publicly.

Q175.L1t: The passage is a humorous story about a boy named Tommy who was weak at math and then improved at a new school.
Q175.L2t: In the story, Tommy's parents had already tried tutors, cards and special learning centers before moving him to a Catholic school.
Q175.L3t: The boy's reason for working so hard was what he saw on the first day: a man nailed to a plus sign, which made him decide the school was serious, and a child who fears this would worry the same could happen to him if he failed.
Q175.L4t: Tommy worked hard at math out of fear, because he thought he might be nailed up himself if he did badly.
Q175.L2f: In the story, Tommy's improvement came mainly from the patient extra lessons given to him by the nuns at the school.
Q175.L3f: The story implies that Tommy took a dislike to the plus sign itself, as a symbol he found ugly and unpleasant, and that this feeling made him study.
Q175.L4f: The last sentence shows that Tommy simply did not like the plus sign.

Q176.L1t: The passage is an informative article about Christmas customs and the figure of Father Christmas.
Q176.L2t: The passage says that Nicholas was a Christian bishop in Turkey in about 285 to 350 A.D. and that little is known about him.
Q176.L3t: The passage as a whole covers the story of the gift-giving magical figure, his origin in St Nicholas, and later views on him, but it is about this one figure, not about all Christmas customs or only about the historical man.
Q176.L4t: The passage is best titled as an account of the legend of Santa Claus, covering how the story arose and how people see him.
Q176.L2f: The passage says that Nicholas was a rich Roman emperor who lived in the fifth century and that historians know a great deal about his life.
Q176.L3f: The passage is mainly a detailed historical biography, with most of its length devoted to proving facts about the real life of the bishop and little to the modern legend or to children's reactions.
Q176.L4f: The best title for the passage is the one about the true history of St Nicholas.
